observation.visible_scene: An overhead orbital view of a Space Shuttle (name 'Atlantis' legible on the wing root) with its payload bay doors open, showing tan/orange cargo canisters and equipment inside. Mounted alongside the shuttle is a large open-ended cylindrical payload (aperture facing the camera) with a small dark sphere tethered to it by a thin line. The whole shuttle-plus-payload assembly floats against a backdrop of Earth's swirling cloud cover. In the later part of the clip a separate silver cylindrical object with a white nose cone appears at the right edge of frame.
visible_changes: The shuttle/payload assembly (doors open, cylinder attached, tethered sphere present) keeps a fixed internal configuration throughout; its parts do not separate or deform.

The assembly drifts slowly within the frame (small downward/rightward shift of the nose, cylinder and tethered sphere between first and last frames), while the cloud background also shifts, so the scene is not a static hold.

Starting around t=2.0 s a distinct cylindrical object enters at the right edge and translates leftward into view, closing the gap toward the shuttle's starboard side; by t=2.67 s it is fully visible but still separated from the shuttle.
The tethered small sphere remains at a roughly constant distance from the open cylinder, moving with the assembly rather than as an independent object.
outside_clip_unknowns: Whether the right-edge cylinder will approach, dock with, or pass the shuttle (motion is still ongoing at the crop end).
What precedes the assembly's drift and what follows after the segment (both ends are arbitrary crops).
The identity/mission of the open cylinder and the entering object.
uncertain_details: It is unclear whether the cloud-field motion and the slight frame drift of the shuttle are due to camera pan/rotation or to orbital motion of the spacecraft; background evidence alone does not settle this.
The entering cylinder's leftward motion is relative to the shuttle; whether it is its own translation or revealed by camera movement cannot be confirmed from the clouds.
Exact orientation/attitude changes of the shuttle are subtle and within the noise of slow drift.
